description: Our project is an interactive platform designed to help kids learn what it's like to be an astronaut. Through fun challenges, simulations, and space missions, users can develop problem-solving skills, learn about space exploration, and experience the basics of astronaut training. Our goal is to make learning about space fun, educational, and accessible for everyone.
summary:
Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is a bilingual, interactive 3D simulator where learners design a spacecraft and decide whether it is ready to fly. In the hangar, students choose components and see how each choice affects mass, power, and life support. A larger solar array, for example, can solve a power shortage while adding mass. During flight, students can pause, compare options, and decide how to respond to events such as a solar storm.

The project addresses a challenge in space education: how can beginners and experienced learners explore the same engineering problem? Nine learning profiles combine age group and prior knowledge. A young learner who wants equations can explore them, while an adult beginner can start with everyday language. Everyone uses the same physics model.

An interactive glossary and direct links to NASA sources help learners connect simulated decisions to real missions. Students practice explaining a design choice, checking its consequences, and revising it based on evidence.

details:
Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is a bilingual, browser-based simulator that lets learners design a spacecraft, test whether it is ready to fly, and make decisions during a mission. In the 3D hangar, learners select a crew capsule, solar panels, life-support equipment, shielding, an engine, and a scientific payload. The simulator calculates the combined mass, power balance, and available reserves. If a scientific instrument draws more power than the panels supply, the learner can install larger panels or choose a less demanding instrument. Both choices can solve the shortage, but they have different consequences for mass and scientific capability.

During flight, events such as solar storms and communication failures pause the simulation. Learners can read or hear the options, predict what each decision will cost, and compare the outcome with their prediction. The Space Classroom offers lessons across seven subject areas. A contextual glossary explains terms where they appear, and links beside historical facts and scientific explanations let students and teachers consult the original NASA sources. The interface identifies which values belong to the educational simulation.

The project’s creative feature is that age and prior knowledge are independent choices. Three age groups and three knowledge levels produce nine learning profiles, all using the same physics model. A young learner with advanced knowledge can investigate a power deficit using equations, while an adult beginner can explore the same problem through a plain-language explanation. Either can change the level of guidance without losing the spacecraft they built or the progress they earned.

We built the application with TypeScript, React, and Three.js for the interface and 3D scenes, Node.js and Express for the server, and Vite for development and production builds. It runs in a web browser without specialized hardware. Design considerations included Spanish and English support, keyboard navigation, narration, captions, reduced motion, and privacy. Younger learners can keep their progress on their device using a generated call sign.

Our intended impact is to help students practice engineering judgment: explain why a design failed, use evidence to choose a revision, and test whether it worked. For teachers, the shared simulation offers a way to discuss one engineering problem with students who need different levels of support.
